lead: A measurement is made at the sensor and needed at the readout; the cable between them is where accuracy is lost. Signal transmission moves the value without noise, lost volts or ground errors. A flow transmitter on a process pipe reports to a control room 200 m away over two wires. This chapter covers the two-wire 4–20 mA loop, its resistance limit, resistance-sensor wiring, and digital links.
prereq: You need signal conditioning for what conditioning does before transmission.

blocks.text: A voltage link is simplest. Cable resistance and receiver input form a divider, so the reading depends on cable length and copper temperature. The ends also sit at different earth potentials; a volt of ground difference adds to a voltage signal and looks like measurement.

A current link avoids both. Every element in a series loop carries the same current. The transmitter sets it; wire resistance changes only the voltage needed to push it, never the value. Ground difference does not change a current.
Two wires carry supply and signal. The transmitter is a current sink: it draws current proportional to the measurement, 4 mA at range bottom to 20 mA at top.
The 4 mA start is a live zero. Zero of measurement is 4 mA, not 0 mA. A loop current of 0 mA then means the loop is broken or the transmitter is dead, so the loop reports its own failure.
The receiver puts a precision sense resistor in the loop and measures its voltage.

blocks.where: V<sub>sense</sub> is the sense-resistor voltage in volts; I is loop current in amperes; R<sub>sense</sub> is the sense resistance in ohms. A 250 Ω resistor gives 1 V at 4 mA and 5 V at 20 mA.

R<sub>loop</sub>,max is total cable plus resistor resistance in ohms; V<sub>supply</sub> is supply voltage in volts; V<sub>min</sub> is minimum voltage the transmitter needs, about 10 V to 12 V. Beyond this, the transmitter cannot reach 20 mA.

sections.h3: Wiring, lead resistance and digital links

blocks.text: Use screened twisted pair. Twisting makes both wires pick up the same interference, which cancels; the screen, earthed at one end, shunts electrostatic noise to ground.

Lead resistance matters for resistance sensors, as the second worked example shows. A 2-wire RTD adds its leads to the element and reads high. A 3-wire connection cancels the lead drop if the leads match. A 4-wire (Kelvin) connection uses current-carrying and voltage-sensing leads separately, so lead resistance disappears.

Digital links carry the value as a number. RS-485 is a cheap differential bus for many instruments on one pair. HART puts a small digital signal on top of 4–20 mA. Fieldbus replaces the analogue value. Fibre suits very long runs and high-voltage isolation; wireless suits moving or remote plant. Hospitals use both: telemetry carries the ECG of a walking patient to the nursing station, and fibre-optic links keep metal cable out of an MRI scanner's field.

figure.caption: A 24 V supply, the transmitter, the cable and a 250 Ω sense resistor form one series loop, so the same 4 to 20 mA flows everywhere and the ADC reads 1 to 5 V. At 20 mA the transmitter needs 10 V and the resistor takes 5 V, which leaves 9 V for the cable: 700 Ω for the whole loop.

examples.question: A 2-wire transmitter runs from 24 V and needs 10 V minimum. The receiver uses a 250 Ω sense resistor. Find maximum loop resistance and receiver voltage range.
steps: At full scale I = 20 mA = 0.020 A.
At 4 mA: V<sub>sense</sub> = 0.004 A × 250 Ω = 1 V.
At 20 mA: V<sub>sense</sub> = 0.020 A × 250 Ω = 5 V.
examples.answer: Total loop resistance must not exceed 700 Ω; the receiver sees 1 V to 5 V.
examples.check:
Vs = 24.0
Vmin = 10.0
Imax = 0.020
Rs = 250.0
Rmax = (Vs - Vmin) / Imax
Vlo = 0.004 * Rs
Vhi = Imax * Rs
print(Rmax)
print(Vlo)
print(Vhi)

examples.question: A Pt100 RTD (0.385 Ω per °C near 0 °C) is 20 m from its transmitter; each lead has 0.75 Ω. (a) Find the error of a 2-wire connection. (b) A 3-wire connection leaves a lead mismatch of 0.05 Ω; find its error. (c) The transmitter is ranged 0 to 150 °C on 4–20 mA and sends 12.4 mA. Find the temperature.
steps: (a) In 2-wire both leads add to the element: 2 × 0.75 = 1.5 Ω. Error = 1.5 / 0.385 = 3.9 °C, read high.
(b) In 3-wire the two lead resistances sit in opposite bridge arms and cancel, leaving only their difference: 0.05 / 0.385 = 0.13 °C.
Check: 4 mA would give 0 °C and 20 mA 150 °C; 12.4 mA is just above mid-current (12 mA, 75 °C), so 78.75 °C is consistent. A 4-wire connection would remove even the 0.13 °C.
examples.answer: The 2-wire connection reads 3.9 °C high, the 3-wire 0.13 °C; 12.4 mA means 78.75 °C.

traps: 0 mA is a fault, not a zero reading. Live zero means bottom of range is 4 mA.
The current is the same everywhere in the loop; wire resistance changes voltage, not current.
A 2-wire RTD reads high by its lead resistance; only a 4-wire connection removes it fully.
R<sub>loop</sub>,max counts cable both ways plus the sense resistor, not cable one way.
4 mA is a real offset (the live zero). It is removed at the receiver when voltage is scaled to engineering units, not by changing anything in the loop.

quiz.q: What current range does a standard two-wire transmitter use?
quiz.a: 4 mA at range bottom, 20 mA at top.
The zero of measurement is carried at 4 mA, so 0 mA signals a fault.

quiz.q: Why does 20 Ω of cable not change a 4–20 mA reading?
quiz.a: All elements are in series, so one current flows through the loop. The 20 Ω extra resistance raises the supply voltage needed, not the current.

quiz.q: A 24 V supply feeds a transmitter needing 12 V minimum; full scale is 20 mA. Find the maximum loop resistance.
A 2-wire RTD reads 1.5 Ω high. Which connection fixes it, and how?
quiz.a: A 4-wire (Kelvin) connection: current flows in one lead pair and voltage is sensed on a current-free pair, so lead resistance drops out. A 3-wire connection reduces the error if leads match.

quiz.q: The voltage across the 250 Ω sense resistor falls to 0 V. What do you conclude?
quiz.a: Loop current is 0 mA, so the loop is broken or the transmitter is dead. It is a fault, not a zero measurement.

beyond: Not for the exam. HART still carries 4–20 mA under its digital signal in most process plants; fieldbus and WirelessHART are replacing the analogue value in new installations. Industry searches: loop-powered transmitter, burden voltage (the voltage dropped across the sense resistor by loop current — the load the transmitter must drive), loop calibrator, NAMUR NE43 fault levels.
